name: Malar-submalar combined implant

lead: A combined malar-submalar implant is a cheek implant shaped to augment both the cheekbone (malar) area and the area beneath it (submalar). It is chosen by people who want more cheek projection and a fuller midface in one device.
Cheek implants are made of solid silicone, porous polyethylene or expanded PTFE, and are placed by a plastic or maxillofacial surgeon.

paras: A surgeon selects an implant shape and size and places it over the cheek bone area, usually through an incision inside the mouth or lower eyelid. Surgeons and patients discuss swelling and recovery over weeks.

General risks include infection, bleeding, swelling and blood clots. Asymmetry from shifting or uneven resorption can occur, and temporary numbness is common. Porous polyethylene can be harder to remove at revision because tissue grows into it [1].

chain: Implant covers cheekbone and submalar area
angle.text: The device physically adds volume over the cheekbone and below it, changing the contour of the midface in one procedure.

lead: The malar-submalar combined implant is a type of cheek implant made longer so that it augments both the cheekbones and the midface hollow below them. It is used to increase cheek projection and fullness for people with flat or sunken midfaces.

Reference descriptions distinguish three shapes: malar implants that sit on the cheekbones to add height, submalar implants that fill the midface, and combined implants that cover both [1]. Common materials are solid silicone, porous polyethylene and expanded PTFE [1].

paras: Combined implants are longer than either single-purpose type and aim to augment both the midface and the cheekbones [1]. Silicone is the most widely used material; polyethylene (Medpor) and ePTFE bond better with surrounding tissue, with the tradeoff that ingrowth can complicate removal [1].
Risks include infection, bleeding, clots and swelling; asymmetry from resorption, displacement or shifting; and temporary numbness, with longer-lasting sensory loss possible [1].
No studies found specific to combined implants in this wiki's research base.
